en.title: `<iostream.h>` → `<iostream>`
en.why: The `.h` C++ headers (`iostream.h`, `fstream.h`, `iomanip.h`) predate the 1998 C++ standard. Turbo C++ accepted them; no modern compiler (GCC, Clang, MSVC) ships them. Standard headers have no `.h`.
en.mistake: Mistake: thinking `<stdio.h>` and `<string.h>` are also wrong. They are C headers and still valid (C++ also offers `<cstdio>`, `<cstring>`).

practice.q: Which include fails on a modern C++ compiler?
practice.explain: `<iostream.h>` only existed in Turbo C++. The other three are standard.

hi.title: `<iostream.h>` → `<iostream>`
hi.why: `.h` wale C++ headers (`iostream.h`, `fstream.h`, `iomanip.h`) 1998 ke C++ standard se pehle ke hain. Turbo C++ unhe chalata tha, par GCC, Clang, MSVC — koi modern compiler unhe nahi jaanta. Naye headers mein `.h` nahi lagta.
hi.mistake: Galti: `<stdio.h>` aur `<string.h>` ko bhi galat samajh lena. Woh C ke headers hain aur ab bhi valid hain (C++ mein unke naye naam `<cstdio>`, `<cstring>` bhi hain).

practice.q: Modern C++ mein inme se kaunsa include ERROR dega?
practice.explain: `<iostream.h>` sirf Turbo C++ mein tha. Baaki teeno standard hain.

en.title: `cout` → `std::cout`
en.why: Every standard library name (`cout`, `cin`, `endl`, `setw`, …) lives in the `std` namespace so it cannot clash with your own names. Turbo C++ had no namespaces. Write `std::` (professional style) or once `using namespace std;`.
en.mistake: Mistake: putting `using namespace std;` in a header — every file that includes it inherits the clash risk. In a small `.cpp` it is fine.

practice.q: After `#include <iostream>` with no `using`, what do you write?
practice.explain: Namespace and member are joined with `::`: `std::cout`.

hi.title: `cout` → `std::cout`
hi.why: Standard library ke saare naam (`cout`, `cin`, `endl`, `setw`, …) `std` namespace mein rehte hain, taaki tumhare apne variables se na takrayein. Turbo C++ mein namespace hote hi nahi the. Ya to har jagah `std::` likho (professional style), ya ek baar `using namespace std;`.
hi.mistake: Galti: header file mein `using namespace std;` likhna — jo bhi us header ko include kare, uske saare naam std se takra sakte hain. `.cpp` mein chhote programs ke liye theek hai.

practice.q: `#include <iostream>` ke baad bina `using` ke kya likhoge?
practice.explain: Namespace ka naam aur member `::` se jodte hain: `std::cout`.

en.title: `void main()` → `int main()`
en.why: Both the C and C++ standards require `main` to return `int` — the number tells the operating system whether the program succeeded (0) or failed. `void main` was a Turbo C allowance. `return 0;` at the end of `main` is optional; the compiler assumes 0. In C, write `int main(void)` — empty brackets in C mean "any arguments".
en.mistake: Mistake: keeping a bare `return;` inside after switching to `int main()` — it must become `return 0;`. PRABHA changes that too.

practice.q: What happens without `return 0;` at the end of `int main()`?
practice.explain: For `main` only, reaching the end is the same as `return 0;`.

hi.title: `void main()` → `int main()`
hi.why: C aur C++ standard dono kehte hain `main` ko `int` return karna hai — ye number operating system ko batata hai program theek khatam hua (0) ya error se. `void main` sirf Turbo C ki chhoot thi. `main` ke end mein `return 0;` likhna optional hai — compiler khud 0 maan leta hai. C mein khaali brackets ki jagah `int main(void)` likhte hain (C mein `()` ka matlab "koi bhi arguments" hota hai).
hi.mistake: Galti: `int main()` banane ke baad bhi andar `return;` (bina value) chhod dena — ab `return 0;` chahiye. PRABHA ye bhi badal deta hai.

practice.q: `int main()` mein end par `return 0;` na likho to kya hoga?
practice.explain: Sirf `main` ke liye standard kehta hai ki end tak pahunchna = `return 0;`.

en.title: Final `getch();` → `std::cin.get();`
en.why: Turbo C closed the output window at once, so programs ended with `getch()` to hold the screen. `getch` comes from non-standard `conio.h`. The standard way is `std::cin.get();` (C++) or `getchar();` (C) — they wait for Enter instead of any key.
en.mistake: Mistake: after `cin >> x;` a `cin.get()` returns at once — the previous Enter is still buffered. Add `cin.ignore();` first. (PRABHA Console already shows "Press any key", so it is not needed there.)

practice.q: Which header provides `getch()`?
practice.explain: `conio.h` — a DOS header, not part of standard C/C++.

hi.title: Aakhri `getch();` → `std::cin.get();`
hi.why: Turbo C mein output window turant band ho jaati thi, isliye end mein `getch()` likhte the "screen rokne" ke liye. `getch` `conio.h` ka hai jo standard nahi. Standard tareeka: C++ mein `std::cin.get();`, C mein `getchar();` — farak sirf itna ki ye Enter ka intezaar karte hain.
hi.mistake: Galti: `cin >> x;` ke baad `cin.get()` turant aage badh jaata hai — kyunki pichhla Enter abhi buffer mein hai. Tab `cin.ignore();` pehle lagao. (PRABHA Console khud "Press any key" dikhata hai, isliye wahan iski zaroorat hi nahi.)

practice.q: `getch()` kis header se aata hai?
practice.explain: `conio.h` — DOS ka header, standard C/C++ ka hissa nahi.

en.title: `clrscr();` removed
en.why: Standard C/C++ has no clear-screen function — the terminal belongs to the OS, not the language. `system("cls")` / `system("clear")` work but are slow and OS-specific, so avoid them while learning. Modern IDEs show fresh output on every run.
en.mistake: REVIEW: this changes what the user sees — the old program cleared the screen, the new one does not. That is why the rule is off by default.

practice.q: Standard C++ function to clear the screen?
practice.explain: There is none in the standard. `clrscr` was Turbo-only.

hi.title: `clrscr();` hataya
hi.why: Standard C/C++ mein screen saaf karne ka koi function nahi hai — terminal OS ka hissa hai, language ka nahi. `system("cls")` / `system("clear")` chalta hai par slow aur OS-specific hai, isliye seekhte waqt use na karna hi behtar. Modern IDEs har run par naya output dikhate hain.
hi.mistake: DHYAAN DO (review): ye badlaav output ka dikhna badalta hai — purana program screen saaf karta tha, naya nahi karega. Isliye ye rule default OFF hai.

practice.q: Standard C++ mein screen clear karne ka function?
practice.explain: Standard mein aisa koi function nahi. `clrscr` Turbo ka tha.

en.title: `#include <conio.h>` removed
en.why: No `conio.h` function is left in the program, so the include is unused. `conio.h` was a DOS header — Linux and macOS do not have it.
en.mistake: Mistake: removing it while `getch()` / `gotoxy()` are still used. PRABHA removes it only when none is left.

practice.q: Which is NOT a `conio.h` function?
practice.explain: `printf` is a standard `<stdio.h>` function.

hi.title: `#include <conio.h>` hataya
hi.why: Program mein ab `conio.h` ka koi function nahi bacha, isliye ye include bekaar hai. `conio.h` DOS ka header tha — Linux aur macOS par hota hi nahi.
hi.mistake: Galti: `getch()` / `gotoxy()` abhi bhi use ho rahe hon aur include hata dena. PRABHA tabhi hatata hai jab koi conio function na bache.

practice.q: Inme se kaunsa `conio.h` ka function NAHI hai?
practice.explain: `printf` `<stdio.h>` ka standard function hai.

en.title: `#include <dos.h>` removed
en.why: Nothing from `dos.h` (delay, sound, getdate…) is left. `dos.h` only existed on DOS.

practice.q: Which header has the modern C++ replacement for `delay()`?
practice.explain: `std::this_thread::sleep_for` is in `<thread>` (durations in `<chrono>`).

hi.title: `#include <dos.h>` hataya
hi.why: Program mein ab `dos.h` ka kuch (delay, sound, getdate…) nahi bacha. `dos.h` sirf DOS par tha.

practice.q: `delay()` ka modern C++ version kis header mein hai?
practice.explain: `std::this_thread::sleep_for` `<thread>` mein hai (time ke liye `<chrono>`).

en.title: `gets()` → `getline` / `fgets`
en.why: `gets()` does not know how big the array is — typing more than fits writes past it (the 1988 Morris Worm used exactly this). C11 and C++14 removed `gets` from the standard. C++: `std::cin.getline(s, sizeof s);`, C: `fgets(s, sizeof s, stdin);` — both respect the size.
en.mistake: Mistake: `fgets` keeps the trailing `\n`. PRABHA adds `s[strcspn(s, "\n")] = '\0';` so the output stays the same.

practice.q: Why was `gets()` removed?
options: Array ki size check nahi karta (buffer overflow)
practice.explain: Not knowing the size causes overflows — a security bug.

hi.title: `gets()` → `getline` / `fgets`
hi.why: `gets()` ko pata hi nahi ki array kitna bada hai — user zyada type kare to memory ke bahar likh deta hai (yahi bug 1988 ke Morris Worm ne use kiya tha). Isliye C11 aur C++14 se `gets` standard se HATA diya gaya. C++: `std::cin.getline(s, sizeof s);`, C: `fgets(s, sizeof s, stdin);` — dono size ka dhyaan rakhte hain.
hi.mistake: Galti: `fgets` line ke end ka `\n` bhi rakh leta hai. PRABHA uske baad `s[strcspn(s, "\n")] = '\0';` jodta hai taaki output pehle jaisa rahe.

practice.q: `gets()` kyun hataya gaya?
options: Array ki size check nahi karta (buffer overflow)
practice.explain: Size na jaanne se overflow — security bug.

en.title: `char name[20]` → `std::string`
en.why: `char name[20]` corrupts memory when a name longer than 19 characters is typed. `std::string` grows on its own and works with `cin >>` / `cout <<` exactly the same. PRABHA only changes it when the variable is used just with `cin >>` and `cout <<`.
en.mistake: Mistake: using `strcpy`/`strlen` on a `std::string`. Strings use `=` and `.length()`.

practice.q: How do you get the length of `std::string s = "Kanak";`?
practice.explain: `s.length()` (or `s.size()`) = 5.

hi.title: `char name[20]` → `std::string`
hi.why: `char name[20]` mein 19 se lamba naam aaye to memory kharab hoti hai. `std::string` apne aap badhti hai, aur `cin >>` / `cout <<` dono ke saath bilkul waise hi chalti hai. PRABHA ye tabhi badalta hai jab variable sirf `cin >>` aur `cout <<` mein use ho.
hi.mistake: Galti: `std::string` ke saath `strcpy`/`strlen` lagana. String mein `=` aur `.length()` use hote hain.

practice.q: `std::string s = "Kanak";` ki length kaise nikaloge?
practice.explain: `s.length()` (ya `s.size()`) = 5.

en.title: `randomize()` / `random(n)` → `srand` / `rand`
en.why: `randomize()` and `random(n)` were Borland-only. The standard way: `std::srand(std::time(nullptr));` once, then `std::rand() % n` (0 to n-1). For serious work `<random>` (`std::mt19937`) is better.
en.mistake: Mistake: calling `srand(time(0))` inside a loop — the same seed gives the same number.

practice.q: What range does `std::rand() % 6` give?
practice.explain: `% 6` yields 0–5. Add 1 for a dice roll.

hi.title: `randomize()` / `random(n)` → `srand` / `rand`
hi.why: `randomize()` aur `random(n)` Borland (Turbo) ke apne functions the. Standard tareeka: `std::srand(std::time(nullptr));` ek baar, phir `std::rand() % n` (0 se n-1). Bade projects ke liye `<random>` (`std::mt19937`) aur behtar hai.
hi.mistake: Galti: `srand(time(0))` ko loop ke andar likhna — har baar same seed, same number.

practice.q: `std::rand() % 6` kin values ke beech aata hai?
practice.explain: `% 6` ka result 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 ya 5. Dice ke liye `+ 1` karo.

en.title: `delay(ms)` → `std::this_thread::sleep_for`
en.why: `delay()` came from `dos.h`. Since C++11 the standard way is `std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(500));` — the same on Windows, Linux and macOS. (graphics.h programs keep PRABHA's `delay`, which also sends animation frames.)
en.mistake: Mistake: treating `sleep(1)` as milliseconds — POSIX `sleep` takes seconds.

practice.q: Wait for half a second:
practice.explain: The duration type must be explicit: `std::chrono::milliseconds(500)`.

hi.title: `delay(ms)` → `std::this_thread::sleep_for`
hi.why: `delay()` `dos.h` ka tha. C++11 se standard tareeka: `std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(500));` — Windows, Linux, macOS sab par same. (graphics.h programs mein PRABHA ka `delay` hi rehta hai, kyunki woh animation frames bhi bhejta hai.)
hi.mistake: Galti: `sleep(1)` ko milliseconds samajhna — POSIX `sleep` seconds leta hai.

practice.q: Aadhe second ke liye ruko:
practice.explain: Duration ka type batana padta hai: `std::chrono::milliseconds(500)`.

en.title: `NULL` → `nullptr`
en.why: In C++ `NULL` is really `0` — an integer, so `f(NULL)` can pick the wrong (int) overload. C++11 `nullptr` can only be a pointer, so no mix-up is possible.
en.mistake: Mistake: `int x = nullptr;` — nullptr cannot become an integer (a compile error, which is the point).

practice.q: How do you write a null pointer in modern C++?
practice.explain: `nullptr` (C++11).

hi.title: `NULL` → `nullptr`
hi.why: C++ mein `NULL` asal mein `0` hai — ek integer. Isliye `f(NULL)` galat overload (int wala) chuna ja sakta hai. C++11 ka `nullptr` sirf pointer ho sakta hai, galti ki gunjaish nahi.
hi.mistake: Galti: `int x = nullptr;` — nullptr integer nahi ban sakta (compile error, aur yahi achhi baat hai).

practice.q: Modern C++ mein null pointer kaise likhte hain?
practice.explain: `nullptr` (C++11).

en.title: `far` / `near` / `huge` removed
en.why: These were keywords for DOS 16-bit segmented memory (64 KB segments). Today's 64-bit machines have one flat address space — the keywords mean nothing and modern compilers do not know them.

practice.q: What does `char far *p` become today?
practice.explain: Just `char *p` — the pointer works the same.

hi.title: `far` / `near` / `huge` hataye
hi.why: Ye DOS ke 16-bit "segmented memory" ke keywords the (64 KB ke segments). Aaj ke 64-bit computers par memory ek flat address space hai — in keywords ka koi matlab nahi, aur modern compiler unhe jaante bhi nahi.

practice.q: `char far *p` aaj kya hoga?
practice.explain: Bas `char *p` — pointer waisa hi kaam karta hai.
